title: Career Planning
summary: Plan your career with confidence: understanding your interests, skills and values, exploring careers and the labour market, education and training pathways, SMART goals and action plans, job search, networking and avoiding scams, and growing or changing careers.
audience: Secondary students, school leavers, graduates and adults planning a career move

body.p: Career planning is an ongoing process of understanding yourself, exploring options, making decisions and taking action, then adjusting as you grow and the world changes. Few people follow a straight line; most change roles or even fields several times. Planning helps you make those changes on purpose rather than by accident.

list: Interests: what activities, subjects and problems do you enjoy and lose track of time doing?
Skills: what are you good at, or could become good at? Include technical skills (accounting, coding, cooking) and transferable skills (communication, organisation, problem-solving).
Values: what matters most to you in work, such as income, security, helping others, creativity, independence or status?
Personality and working style: do you prefer working with people, data, things or ideas; in teams or alone; in a routine or with variety?

body.p: Free online interest inventories, such as tools based on Holland's RIASEC types (realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising and conventional), can give ideas, but treat results as starting points, not instructions.

body.tip: Ask three people who know you well what they see as your strengths; their answers often surprise you.

lessons.title: Explore careers and the labour market

list: Research careers: what people do daily, the qualifications needed, typical pay, working conditions and future demand.
Look at the labour market: which sectors are growing in your country and region, such as digital services, renewable energy, health care, agribusiness, logistics and the creative industries.
Speak to people in the field through informational interviews: short conversations to learn about their work, not to ask for a job.
Try work: job shadowing, volunteering, internships, learnerships, part-time jobs and small projects reveal what you enjoy.

body.p: In many African economies, a large share of people work in the informal sector or are self-employed. Entrepreneurship, freelancing and remote work for international clients are real career paths alongside formal employment, and many people combine several income sources.

body.tip: Search job adverts for roles that interest you, even if you are not ready to apply, and list the skills they repeatedly ask for.

body.p: There are many routes into good careers; university is only one of them.

list: University degrees for professions such as medicine, law, engineering and teaching.
Technical and vocational education and training (TVET) colleges and polytechnics for trades and technical careers, often with strong job prospects.
Apprenticeships and learnerships combining workplace learning with study.
Short courses and online certificates, such as in digital skills, which can quickly add employable skills.
Learning on the job and through mentors.

body.p: Check accreditation: make sure the institution and qualification are recognised by the relevant national authority and employers. Compare costs, duration, entry requirements and graduate outcomes. Look for bursaries, scholarships, loans and employer sponsorship. If a course costs R12 000 and you have a year to prepare, saving R1000 a month gets you there.

body.tip: Beware of unaccredited institutions that promise guaranteed jobs; verify before paying.

lessons.title: Setting goals and making a plan

body.p: Turn ideas into action with SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. "Get a better job" becomes "Complete a bookkeeping certificate by June and apply for five junior accounts jobs a week from July".

steps: Write a long-term goal (three to five years).
Break it into medium-term milestones (one year).
List short-term actions for the next month.
Identify resources and people who can help.
Set review dates to check progress and adjust.

body.p: Spending 5 hours a week on learning adds up to 5 x 4 x 12 = 240 hours a year, enough to build serious skills in a new area. If you send 20 applications and a quarter lead to interviews, that is 5 interviews, so persistence matters.

body.tip: Have a plan B: if your first-choice path is closed for now, choose a related route that keeps you moving towards your goal.

list: Prepare a clear, honest CV tailored to each role, highlighting achievements with evidence.
Write a short cover letter that explains why you fit this specific job.
Use professional networking sites such as LinkedIn, and keep your profile up to date.
Network through alumni groups, professional associations, events and community connections. Many jobs are filled through referrals.
Prepare for interviews by researching the organisation and practising answers using examples from your experience.

body.p: Be cautious of offers that ask you to pay for a job, training or a uniform, promise very high pay for little work, or come only through messaging apps from unknown recruiters. Verify the company, and never share bank details or ID documents until you are sure an offer is genuine. Fake overseas job offers can lead to exploitation and trafficking.

body.tip: Keep a simple tracker of applications: date, role, company, status and follow-up.

body.p: Career planning continues after you get a job.

list: Keep learning: technology and industries change fast, so update skills regularly.
Seek feedback and stretch assignments to grow.
Find mentors, and later mentor others.
Build a reputation for reliability, integrity and good work.
Review your career plan at least once a year.

body.p: Career changes are normal. Identify your transferable skills, test a new field through a side project or short course, and build connections before making the leap. Save some money first if possible, to give yourself time to make the transition.
A good career supports a good life. Pay attention to health, relationships and rest, and recognise burnout signs such as constant exhaustion and loss of motivation.

body.tip: Write a short career story: where you have been, what you have learned and where you are heading. It helps in interviews and decisions.
